problems.description: add_task removes the existing 400 validation guard and uses request.json['title'] directly; a missing/invalid body raises KeyError/TypeError producing a 500 instead of a graceful 400. This contradicts the retained test_post_missing_json which still asserts 400, leaving code and tests inconsistent.

test fixture drops the tasks table in teardown rather than setup; combined with a module-level NamedTemporaryFile shared across tests, a test failure before teardown leaks state into subsequent tests (e.g., the hardcoded id==1 assertions break).
test_list_tasks_ordered asserts data[0]=='Task 3' order, tightly coupling the test to the underlying ORDER BY implementation; a reordering query change silently breaks the suite.

Convention score 0.67 and 11 violations are largely attributed to files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repository.py, tasks.py, __init__.py); only the app.py PascalCase item is in-scope, so the measurement overstates this commit's own deviation.

strengths: Fixes a genuine bug: hardcoded status='done' corrected to 'pending' in create_task.
Adds substantial coverage (127 lines, 13 test functions) for CRUD, 404s, empty bodies, and id monotonicity using the app's existing test_client.
Reuses existing create_task/get_db/app structure rather than restructuring the module.
New tests follow snake_case and standard pytest fixture conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: Fixes a real status bug and adds solid coverage, but the regression is the removal of input validation (trading a 400 for an unhandled 500 that contradicts a kept test), and the mechanical 0.67 convention score is inflated by violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: ALTER TABLE adds owner_id with no NOT NULL or FOREIGN KEY; all pre-existing tasks have NULL owner_id and become invisible to every user (data access regression for existing rows)
SECRET_KEY silently falls back to a hardcoded dev key when env var is unset, allowing token forgery if deployed without configuration
create_task/get_tasks/get_task signatures changed; fetch_task alias is retained for legacy clients but its signature changed too, so it no longer preserves backward compatibility
No tests added for the new auth routes, owner_id scoping, or the NULL-owner migration path
add_task uses request.json['title'] (raises on missing key) while register uses get_json(silent=True), an inconsistent error-handling pattern introduced within the same commit
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated (pre-existing pattern, extended into the new JWT exp claim)

strengths: Every task query is now scoped by owner_id, providing real tenant data isolation
Idiomatic auth: bcrypt password hashing, JWT with exp claim, login_required decorator using Flask g and wraps
Consistent with existing codebase style: section-comment layout, snake_case functions, type hints on public signatures
Correct HTTP semantics (400/401/404/409) and retains legacy helpers with clear comments
commit_reviews.summary: Solid feature addition that respects the single-file Flask structure and existing patterns, but ships a hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback and a nullable owner_id that orphans pre-existing tasks.

problems.description: Notification side effect embedded directly in the edit_task route handler rather than isolated in a service/use-case layer; this couples HTTP logic to async job dispatch and is the main driver of the +35 cognitive complexity delta.
Magic string comparison data.get('status') == 'completed' — status values are compared as bare literals with no shared enum/constant.
register() silently fabricates a default email f'{username}@example.com' when none is provided, storing invented user data in the DB.
New Celery+Redis broker dependency has no graceful degradation path in the app if the broker is unreachable (only tests opt into task_always_eager).
tasks.py uses both print(msg) and logger.info(msg) redundantly.

Convention score 0.67 / 11 violations: most are SonarQube style false-positives (module-level constants like BROKER_URL already UPPER_CASE; violations attributed to repository.py and __init__.py are not touched by this diff) — treat as pre-existing noise rather than regressions.

strengths: Follows existing module patterns: get_user_by_id mirrors get_user_by_username, register() extends create_user() naturally, and the idempotent ALTER TABLE migration guards match the established init_db style.
Excellent test discipline: 5 targeted notification tests covering trigger, non-trigger (other status, title-only), 404, and custom-email paths, all using mock.patch and the existing fixture pattern.
CELERY_ALWAYS_EAGER env switch cleanly decouples test environment from a live broker — the right seam for testing async tasks.
Clean separation of concerns for the new subsystem: celery_config.py (infra config) vs tasks.py (task definition) vs app.py (dispatch), with task_routes keeping jobs on a dedicated queue.
SonarQube smells -4 and bugs +0, with zero duplication introduced.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-consistent integration of Celery-based email notifications that is architecturally sound for this small app, though it embeds the side effect directly in the route handler and takes a minor hit on convention style that is largely pre-existing measurement noise.

problems.description: Convention score of 0.67 is dragged down by violations in files this commit did not touch (tasks.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py). Only repository.py module-level constants and app.py class naming fall on the changed surface, and app.py's violation appears pre-existing since the diff adds only PascalCase class instances.
BaseRepository(ABC) declares no abstract methods, making the ABC base decorative; either add @abstractmethod hooks or drop the ABC to avoid a misleading contract.

No test changes accompany the refactor even though every route's data-access call was renamed (create_task->task_repo.create, get_task->find_by_id_and_owner, etc.); tests should lock in behavior-preservation.
Repositories are instantiated at module import time in app.py with get_db injected by hand; acceptable for this Flask app, but wiring is spread across two call sites rather than centralized.
SonarQube smells +7 in the change; minor and fully offset by the -26 cognitive-complexity reduction.

strengths: Extracts all data access into TaskRepository/UserRepository, cleanly separating SQL from Flask route logic.
Removes dead code and legacy stubs (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias), shrinking the file by 101 lines.
Cuts cognitive complexity by 26 with zero new bugs and no duplication, keeping public route behavior intact.
No new dependencies; reuses the existing get_db() context-manager seam, so the refactor stays idiomatic to the codebase.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean repository-pattern refactor that reduces complexity by 26 and deletes dead code with no behavior change; the 0.67 convention score overstates the commit's own issues because most violations are pre-existing in untouched files, and the +7 smells are minor and offset by the complexity win.

problems.description: Keyset pagination mismatch: cursor filters `id < ?` but rows are ordered by `created_at DESC, id DESC`. If created_at ever diverges from id monotonicity (backdated/equal-timestamp rows), items can be silently skipped or duplicated across pages. A composite cursor on (created_at, id) or pure id ordering would be keyset-correct.
`_rate_limit_key` uses a bare `except Exception: pass` around JWT decode, silently swallowing all errors; should narrow to `jwt.InvalidTokenError` so real failures surface.
`find_all_by_owner` becomes dead code after the route switches to the paginated variant; consider removing it or routing the paginated call through it.

flask-limiter defaults storage to `redis://localhost:6379/0`, so importing app.py fails if Redis is down unless RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI is set; tests sidestep this with `memory://` but the runtime default is fragile.
Breaking change to the `/tasks` response shape (list → `{data, next_cursor, total}` envelope) without versioning; acceptable for this baseline, but all consumers must change simultaneously.

strengths: Cursor pagination with proper has_more detection (LIMIT limit+1) and clamped limit (1–100)
Per-user rate limiting via JWT-derived key with IP fallback and env-driven storage URI
Comprehensive pagination tests (default/custom/max limit, cursor traversal) plus updated existing tests
Follows existing repository pattern, reusing `_fetchone`/`_fetchall` helpers
SonarQube: −3 smells, −4 cognitive complexity, 0 new bugs and 0% duplication
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting change that adds keyset pagination and per-user rate limiting with strong test coverage and cleaner SonarQube metrics, marred only by a minor cursor-ordering mismatch and dead code.
